01

Estimate the effect of replacing one assessment mark

The grade improvement calculator models a specific change: one existing assessment score is removed and replaced by a new score at the same course weight. It shows the revised weighted course percentage and the change from the current percentage.

This is useful for exploring an authorized reassessment, a corrected marking error, or a hypothetical improvement before discussing available options. It does not grant a resubmission, request a regrade, or decide which result your institution will count. Before treating a scenario as a likely outcome, confirm whether replacement is allowed and whether the replacement mark is capped, averaged with the original, or subject to another rule.

02

Make sure the current grade already includes the old score

Enter a current course percentage that already contains the existing assessment at its stated full-course weight. Then enter the old assessment percentage, the proposed replacement percentage, and the assessment's weight as a percentage of the full course.

The model needs a consistent weighted total, not a normalized average covering an unrelated completed subset. If a gradebook shows an average only across completed work, the assessment's effective weight within that display may differ from its full-course weight. Reconstruct a consistent total first. All score inputs must lie between zero and one hundred, and the assessment weight must be positive and no greater than one hundred.

03

Only the changed contribution needs to be adjusted

Revised course grade = Current grade + (Replacement score − Existing score) × Weight / 100.

The difference between new and old scores tells you the assessment-level change. Multiplying by the course-weight fraction converts that change into course percentage points. Adding it to the current course grade preserves the contribution of all other work.

This shortcut works because the assessment weight stays fixed and the old score was already included once. It does not add an extra assessment or increase the total course weight. A lower replacement produces a negative change. Whether a lower mark would actually replace a higher one is a policy question for your instructor, not a calculation setting here.

04

A thirty-point assessment improvement adds six course points

Suppose your current course grade is 75%. It includes an assessment worth 20% of the course that originally scored 60%. Replacing that assessment mark with 90% improves the assessment by thirty points. The course gain is 30 × 0.20 = 6 percentage points, producing a revised grade of 81%.

You can also verify by separating contributions. The old assessment supplied 60 × 0.20 = 12 course points. All other work therefore supplied 75 − 12 = 63. The replacement supplies 90 × 0.20 = 18. Add 63 and 18 to recover 81. Both methods describe the same replacement without counting the assessment twice.

The six-point gain is an absolute course percentage-point change. It is not a six-percent relative increase: moving from 75 to 81 is an eight-percent increase relative to the original seventy-five. Keep that distinction clear when comparing results.

05

Weight determines how much an improvement matters

A ten-point rise on an assessment worth 10% raises the course grade by one percentage point. The same assessment-level improvement at 40% weight raises it by four course points. The percentage printed on the assessment and its influence on the course are separate quantities.

With a current course grade of 75%, an old score of 60%, and a 20% assessment weight, replacing the score with 80% gives 79% overall. A replacement of 90% gives 81%, and 100% gives 83%. The maximum gain from this assessment is therefore eight course points under these inputs. Improvements elsewhere or changes to other rules are outside this single-replacement scenario.

06

Why some combinations are inconsistent

The calculator checks the contribution implied for other coursework. In the previous example, the other 80% supplies 63 course points, equivalent to a 78.75% average across that block. That is feasible within a zero-to-one-hundred scoring range.

Consider instead a current grade of 10%, an old assessment score of 100%, and an assessment weight of 50%. The assessment alone would already contribute fifty course points. Other work would need a negative contribution to reach ten, so those inputs cannot describe the assumed course. An error usually means the current total has a different basis, the old score was excluded, or the assessment weight was entered incorrectly.

07

Distinguish replacement from adding another attempt

Some retake policies count both attempts, some average the attempts, and some keep only the higher score. This tool performs a full replacement regardless of which new percentage is entered. Do not use it to represent a different rule without first calculating the score that the policy actually records.

A reassessment cap can change the replacement input. If a raw retake score is 85% but the officially counted replacement is capped at another value, enter the counted percentage once you have confirmed it. Category-level changes can also be more complex: replacing one quiz within a quiz category requires determining its actual effective course weight, not assigning the whole category weight to that single quiz.

08

Use a scenario to prepare a focused conversation

Compare a few plausible replacement scores and note the corresponding course changes. This helps you understand what one authorized correction could accomplish. Pair the estimate with assessment feedback, the relevant deadline, and the exact replacement rule when asking an instructor about next steps.

For several eligible replacements, calculate one at a time using each revised total as the next starting point, only if all weights stay fixed and every old score remains included in that total. Keep a clear record of the sequence. If the issue concerns GPA and repeated courses rather than a percentage inside one course, the retake GPA calculator addresses that different question.

Quick answers

Frequently asked questions

Can I enter a lower replacement score?

Yes. The formula can show a decrease as well as an improvement. Whether a lower attempt would actually be recorded depends on your course policy. The calculator does not automatically retain the better score.

Does changing one mark guarantee the displayed course result?

No. The estimate assumes a consistent current total, a full replacement, and unchanged weights. Official results may apply caps, rounding, excluded work, or separate pass requirements that are not represented in those four inputs.

What weight should I use for one quiz inside a category?

Use the quiz’s effective weight in the full course, after accounting for its share of the category. For example, one of four equally weighted quizzes in a 20% category has a 5% full-course weight.

Can I use this for a new assignment not previously graded?

No. This calculator removes an old contribution and substitutes a new one. A genuinely new assessment changes the completed record in another way. Use a weighted-grade calculation or a remaining-work target appropriate to the grading system.
